candidates.title: High-loading all-solid-state lithium–sulfur batteries enabled by tailored sulfur–sulfide and sulfur–carbon interfaces
candidates.authors: Yukio Cho, Hongchang Hao, Miso Kim, Madison King, Zisheng Zhang, Shripad Patil, Jason Hwong, Haoyu Liu, Duhan Zhang, Yifan Quan, Xueli Zheng, Yan-Kai Tzeng, Bonggeun Shong, John Watt, Frank Abild-Pedersen, William C. Chueh, Yi Cui, Stacey F. Bent, Jagjit Nanda
candidates.abstract: High energy density promised by solid-state batteries requires overcoming fundamental limitations in carrier transport. Although tortuous carrier pathways in high-loading cathodes are often viewed as the dominant bottleneck, we show that interfacial ion and electron transport is an even more critical lever for enhancing energy density in sulfide-based all-solid-state lithium–sulfur batteries. By enabling partial lithiation at the sulfur–sulfide interface and eliminating the electron-impeding oxidation layer at the sulfur–carbon interface, we achieve high-loading all-solid-state lithium–sulfur battery cathodes with areal capacities near 15 mAh cm−2 and sulfur utilization above 90% with a moderate stack pressure of 15–25 MPa. These metrics correspond to projected pouch-cell-level energy densities surpassing 500 Wh kg−1. Fast cycling at 1C retains 82.1% capacity over 500 cycles with Coulombic efficiencies up to 99.9%, and stable cycling is also achieved with a lithium metal anode at 10 MPa instead of the more common Li–In alloy. This work highlights the power of interfacial control within composite cathodes, and demonstrates another approach for designing high-energy-density all-solid-state lithium–sulfur batteries for next-generation energy storage. All-solid-state lithium–sulfur batteries are a next-generation high-energy-density solution for energy storage. Here catholyte/cathode interfaces are found to be as important as transport tortuosity in thick sulfur cathodes, and an areal capacity of 10 mAh cm−2 is demonstrated at a stack pressure of 15 MPa and sulfur loading of 6.1 mg cm−2.

candidates.title: Hyperelastic microfibers as bioinspired proprioceptive artificial muscles
candidates.authors: Joonhee Won, Jaehyun Jang, Hyunseo Kim, Inyoung Choi, Kyunghyun Jo, Yunheum Lee, Jiheong Kang, Steve Park, Gun-Hee Lee, Yong-Lae Park, Hyunwoo Yuk, Carmel Majidi, Seongjun Park
candidates.abstract: Abstract Skeletal muscles combine forceful contraction with built-in sensing of their own length and movement, known as proprioception. Reproducing this combination in soft artificial muscles remains difficult, because added sensors often reduce actuation performance, complicate fabrication or limit miniaturization. In natural muscle, specialized sensory fibers are embedded alongside, and mechanically coupled to, the force-generating fibers. Inspired by this arrangement, we pair a hyperelastic, highly stretchable fluid channel with a stiffer, off-center optical core inside a single thin fiber. When liquid is pumped in, the channel wall undergoes a shape bifurcation: a localized bulge forms and propagates along the fiber. Because the core resists stretching, the bulge bends the fiber into a contracting coil, while the core also reports the fiber’s shape through the light it transmits. Here we show that such fibers, produced continuously by a scalable drawing process, act as artificial muscles that sense their own contraction and stretching, supporting self-monitoring movement in soft robots.

candidates.title: Twist-engineered arbitrary polarization detection for intelligent polarimetric sensing
candidates.authors: Mengdie Shi, Tao Ye, Jie Deng, Ruowen Wang, Yonghao Bu, Tianyuan Cui, Liwen Fu, Junwei Huang, Jun Ning, Xueling Guo, Haibo Shu, Xiaoshuang Chen, Jing Zhou
candidates.abstract: Twist-photonics offers a powerful route to engineer light-matter interactions beyond conventional planar architectures. Although twist-photonic platforms, including twist-stacked metasurfaces, van der Waals (vdW) materials and photonic crystals have successfully engineered chiral optical responses, anomalous dispersion and high-Q localized modes, most platforms remain passive. Their translation into on-chip optoelectronic sensing is hindered by an intrinsic trade-off: photosensitive absorbers can quench twist-engineered resonances, whereas passive twist-photonic modes often couple inefficiently to active photocarrier-generation regions. Here, we report an emerging twist-photonic paradigm that integrates anisotropic metasurfaces with anisotropic black phosphorus (BP). Coupled to a vectorial cavity, this twisted stack produces quasi-pure circular-polarization photoresponses and enables arbitrary polarization selectivity across the full Poincaré sphere at multiple wavelengths. Then, we establish an ultra-compact on-chip full-Stokes polarimeter using only two metasurface-BP twisted stacks, achieving high-accuracy full-Stokes reconstruction with a root-mean-square error below 1.3%, and the highest responsivity among reported vdW material-based full-Stokes polarimeters. We further implement an in-sensor kernel matrix that directly maps polarization states into synaptic weights for polarization-programmable multimodal convolutional image processing, reducing electrical switching energy by 1 to 3 orders of magnitude and reconfiguration latency by 2 to 4 orders of magnitude, as the array scales from the 10k-pixel to megapixel level. Twist-photonics can tailor light-matter interactions but is difficult to integrate into active devices. Here, the authors show a twist-stacked plasmonic metasurface-black phosphorus platform for arbitrary polarization detection, full-Stokes sensing, and polarization-programmable in-sensor computing.

candidates.title: SMC5/6 safeguards chromatin compartments and TAD boundaries for genome stability
candidates.authors: Raquel Sofia Silva, Alessandro Morea, Giovanni Lembo, Aki Nunomiya, Federica Lucini, Fabio Iannelli, Nicola Crosetto, Francesco Ferrari, Dana Branzei
candidates.abstract: SMC5/6, a member of the Structural Maintenance of Chromosomes family, coordinates 3D genome organization, chromatin states, and transcriptional regulation, yet its role in higher-order chromatin architecture remains poorly defined. Here, we investigate the impact of conditional SMC5 depletion in human B lymphoblastoid cells. Hi-C analyses reveal global rewiring of chromatin interactions, with increased long-range and reduced short-range contacts, leading to altered large-scale chromosome organization. SMC5 loss induces changes in 3D genome compartmentalization affecting ~2% of the genome and is accompanied by transcriptional upregulation of inflammatory and cancer-associated gene programs. SMC5 depletion also promotes double-strand break accumulation, preferentially in active compartments and following gene expression levels. However, regions undergoing architectural reorganization display comparatively fewer breaks, indicating that chromatin changes are not driven by DNA damage. Together, our findings establish SMC5/6 as a key regulator of chromatin compartmentalization and TAD boundary integrity, linking 3D genome organization to transcriptional control and genome stability. The SMC5/6 complex protects genome stability, but how it shapes 3D genome folding is unclear. Here, the authors show that SMC5/6 loss in human cells alters chromatin compartments and activates inflammatory and cancer-related genes, changes that are uncoupled from DNA damage.

candidates.authors: Youcheng Yang, Yan-Ruide Li, Zeyang Liu, Hao Zhou, Yichen Zhu, Xinyuan Shen, Dexter Lai, Yihui Cen, Emily Z. Y. Miller, Haochen Nan, Bo Zhang, Shubing Wang, Jason Lin, Yuning Chen, Bella Raykowski, Enbo Zhu, Jun Shen, Keyue Shen, Junyoung O. Park, Jingyi Jessica Li, Xiling Shen, Zhaohui Wang, Lili Yang, Song Li
candidates.abstract: Abstract Adoptive T cell receptor (TCR)–based immunotherapy offers a powerful strategy to target solid tumors. However, how the physical properties of the antigen-presenting interface regulate T cell metabolic programming remains poorly defined. Here we develop synthetic viscoelastic activating cells (SynVAC), artificial antigen-presenting cells whose stress-relaxation kinetics are chemically tuned independently of stiffness and of peptide–MHC (pMHC) and co-stimulatory ligand density. SynVAC-pMHC provides a defined, scalable platform that outperforms monocyte-derived dendritic cells to enrich antigen-specific CD8 + T cells. Fast-relaxing SynVAC-pMHC amplifies TCR signaling and mTOR activity, drives metabolic changes, and programs antigen-specific T cells toward an energetically favorable state with improved memory-like features after expansion. TCR-T cells expanded using fast-relaxing SynVAC-pMHC exhibit superior persistence and durable antitumor activity in melanoma and ovarian cancer models. These results establish cell-mimetic viscoelasticity as a key biophysical cue governing T cell metabolism and differentiation and offer a fully synthetic strategy for manufacturing potent TCR-T cells.

candidates.title: Efficient n–i–p all-perovskite tandem solar cells enabled by interconnection layer engineering
candidates.authors: Min Ju Jeong, Dong Hyun Kim, Soo Woong Jeon, Mun Young Woo, Seok Beom Kang, Sangheon Lee, Yeo Jin Choi, Changyong Kim, Sung Yong Kim, Jeong Hyeon Park, Oui Jin Oh, Dong Hoe Kim, Jin Young Kim, Jun Hong Noh
candidates.abstract: All-perovskite tandem solar cells promise ultrahigh efficiencies, yet monolithic devices have been realized predominantly in the p–i–n architecture because n–i–p integration imposes stringent materials constraints. The preformed wide-bandgap top subcell and its hole-selective contact must withstand bottom-subcell fabrication temperatures, limiting material choices. Here we address this challenge using a 2.0 eV Cs-based all-inorganic wide-bandgap subcell and an additive-free P3HT hole-selective contact whose molecular organization is reconfigured by MeO-2PACz. This interfacial modification enhances P3HT ordering and promotes efficient hole extraction, alleviating a transport bottleneck in monolithic n–i–p tandems. candidates.title: A spectral framework for revealing the hidden low-dimensional structure in stochastic reaction networks
candidates.authors: Ankit Gupta, Mustafa Khammash
candidates.abstract: Abstract Stochastic reaction networks govern noise-driven dynamics in systems ranging from gene regulation to cellular signalling and population processes. Yet their high dimensionality and sensitivity to initial states obscure transient mechanisms and limit reliable inference from experimental data. Here, we show that stochastic reaction networks in biological systems often exhibit dominant low-dimensional spectral structure that shapes their dynamics. We develop a spectral framework based on the stochastic Koopman operator that identifies these dominant dynamical modes directly from simulated trajectories, yielding reduced representations with computable error bounds. This reduction enables accurate analytical descriptions of the time evolution of moments, parameter sensitivities, and cross-spectral densities, while achieving order-of-magnitude computational gains relative to standard simulation-based methods. Applied to synthetic gene circuits, our framework reveals the spectral organisation of stochastic oscillators, enables systematic comparison of competing intracellular controllers, and facilitates inference of initial-state distributions from single-cell snapshot population data collected over time. Together, these results establish a principled spectral description of stochastic reaction dynamics and provide a foundation for analysing and inferring high-dimensional noise-driven biological systems.

candidates.authors: Yiwei Duo, Da Huo, Jingnan Dong, Shenyuan Yang, Qichao Yang, Jiaxin Liu, Yifei Yang, Biao Zhang, Tiankuo Zhang, Junxue Ran, Jianchang Yan, Junxi Wang, Peng Gao, Jinmin Li, Zhaolong Chen, Tongbo Wei
candidates.abstract: Two-dimensional materials hold immense potential for memristive devices, offering a pathway to overcome the von Neumann bottleneck. Specifically, hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) is highly promising for low-voltage, multilevel memristors due to its robust physicochemical properties. However, synthesizing wafer-scale, transferable, and thickness-controllable h-BN (tens of nanometers thick) remains challenging, impeding its device integration. Herein, we demonstrate an interfacial modulation strategy via controlled sapphire substrate nitridation to grow high-quality, crack-free h-BN membranes. Introducing an interfacial B–O buffer layer improves the crystalline quality of epitaxial h-BN and facilitates its rapid, damage-free wet transfer onto target substrates. The fabricated memristors with these transferred membranes exhibit a low set voltage of 1.06 V, an ultrahigh ON/OFF ratio of 1.57×109, an ultrafast switching speed of 30 ns, robust multilevel switching and long-term stability. Our study presents a scalable approach for advancing next-generation in-memory computing architectures. candidates.title: Highly elastic ceramic fibers with a high tensile fracture strain
candidates.authors: Yongshi Guo, Jiawei Wu, Yongyong Cao, Hongti Zhang, Wang Hay Kan, Xiaohua Zhang, Yanyan Ma, Xinyu Li, Zheng Yang, Leiming Guo, Tanglong Bai, Jie Sun, Kun Kelvin Fu, Feng Jiang, Chenglong Qiu, Jianhua Yan
candidates.abstract: Ceramics are prized for high strength, but their inherent brittleness has long been a fundamental bottleneck. Here, we overcome this limitation by reporting macroscopically elastic SiO2 fibers that achieve a high tensile fracture strain of 13.59% while maintaining high strength of 1.22 GPa. This is enabled via a metal-coordination-mediated topology reconstruction strategy. We transform the conventional, densely cross-linked Si–O ring network into a low cross-linking structure containing high-density nanopores ( < 3 nm). This structure induces relaxation within the Si–O network—shortening bond lengths and increasing bond angles—which collectively activates an elastic flow behavior, allowing chemical bonds to freely rotate and stretch at low energy. During macroscopic deformation of fibers, the covalent chemical bonds ensure strength, while the nanopore network provides reversible elasticity by efficiently storing and releasing elastic strain energy. Moreover, aerogels fabricated from these fibers synergize super-high elasticity with ultra-low thermal conductivity, showing superb extreme thermal protection property. This work provides a strategy for imparting super-elasticity to traditionally brittle ceramics, achieved through the design of a high-density nanopore network combined with bond modulation. Researchers report elastic SiO2 ceramic fibers with 13.59% tensile strain and 1.23 GPa fracture strength, created by a nanoporous, low-crosslinked Si–O network. These fibers enable super-elastic, highly-insulating aerogels for extreme thermal protection.

candidates.title: Probing Fractional Quantum Hall States in Weakly Interacting Fermi Gases
candidates.authors: Viktor Bekassy, Mikael Fogelström, Johannes Hofmann
candidates.abstract: Quantum gases are used to simulate the physics of the lowest Landau level with neutral atoms, which in the simplest setup is achieved by rotating the gas at the confining harmonic trap frequency, a requirement that is difficult to meet in practice. However, it is known that lowest Landau level states appear among the excited states of weakly interacting gases, even in a nonrotating trap, by working at fixed finite angular momentum. Thus, even in the absence of rotations or for moderate rotation frequencies, fractional quantum Hall (FQH) states can be accessed as excited states at finite angular momentum. Motivated by this, and by recent experimentally demonstrated excitation protocols for two particles, we show that such states can be selectively addressed at larger particle numbers, and we propose imaging techniques to resolve their distinct microscopic structure. In particular, we suggest that recently developed excitation and imaging techniques for rotating few-fermion systems allow for a detailed experimental investigation of FQH wave functions and of the crossover to large particle numbers. We illustrate the evolution of the excitation spectrum with rotations at weak interactions for N = 6 spin-balanced fermions and show how sampling of the few-body wave function allows one to discriminate between total guiding-center, center-of-mass vortex, and hyperradial excitations, thus providing detailed and versatile probes of the microscopic structure of FQH states.

candidates.authors: Sudipta Pattanayak, Alfredo Sciortino, Laurent Blanchoin, Manuel Théry, Jean-François Joanny
candidates.abstract: We propose an active Cahn-Hilliard theory for the dynamics of a new type of phase transition where the driving force is not the direct interactions between the two separating components, but their active sorting by a third polar species. This third species can transport the other two along its polarity in opposite directions, thus separating them. Inspired by recent experiments where molecular motors that walk in opposite directions along microtubules are sorted into separated domains, our theoretical description of this process introduces a new mechanism for active phase separation and could serve as a model for the organization of biological material in space inside cells. We predict the formation of motor domains, and further show that they can either coarsen to form macroscopic phases or reach a finite micro- or mesoscopic steady state size, these latter due to an arrest of coarsening through activity.

candidates.authors: Yidi Liu, Bai Yang Wang, Jiarui Li, Yaoju Tarn, Lopa Bhatt, Michael Colletta, Yi-Ming Wu, Sang-Jun Lee, Cheng-Tai Kuo, Jun-Sik Lee, Berit H. Goodge, David A. Muller, Zhi-Xun Shen, Srinivas Raghu, Harold Y. Hwang, Yijun Yu
candidates.abstract: Understanding how superconductivity emerges and collapses in correlated electron systems remains a central challenge in condensed matter physics. As a recently discovered member of the high temperature superconductor family, bilayer nickelates provide a new opportunity for examining this problem. Their pronounced sensitivity to oxygen stoichiometry, while posing challenges for stabilizing superconductivity, simultaneously offers an effective control parameter for tuning electronic phases. Here we report a superconducting half-dome in compressively strained bilayer nickelate thin films as a function of continuous tuning of oxygen stoichiometry. Starting from an optimally superconducting state, increasing oxygen stoichiometry gradually suppresses superconductivity toward a metallic phase, whereas decreasing oxygen stoichiometry drives a granular superconductor-to-insulator transition while leaving the superconducting onset intact. This half-dome structure is consistent with the contrasting roles played by interstitial oxygen versus oxygen vacancies—namely, the dominance of doping versus scattering. Notably, the half-dome emerges consistently across samples with different rare-earth combinations, with or without alkaline-earth doping, revealing a general feature of the bilayer nickelate phase diagram and informing opportunities for further enhancing superconductivity.

candidates.title: Controlling Energy Delivery with Bistable Nanostructures
candidates.authors: Andreas Ehrmann, Carl P. Goodrich
candidates.abstract: Countless biological processes are fueled by energy-rich molecules like adenosine triphosphate (ATP) and guanosine triphosphate that supply energy with extreme efficiency. However, designing similar energy-delivery schemes from the bottom up, essential for the development of powered nanostructures and other machinery, presents a significant challenge: how can an energy-rich structure be stable in solution yet still deliver this energy at precisely the right time? In this paper, we present a purely physical mechanism that solves this challenge, facilitating energy transfer akin to ATP hydrolysis, yet occurring between synthetic nanostructures without any biochemical interactions. This targeted energy delivery is achieved by exploiting a differentiable state-based model to balance the energy profiles that govern the structural transitions in the two nanostructures, creating a coupled relaxation pathway with minimal barriers that facilitates energy delivery. We verify the effectiveness and robustness of this mechanism through Langevin dynamics simulations demonstrating that a bath of the high-energy structures can systematically and repeatedly drive the target structure out of equilibrium, enabling it to perform tasks. As the mechanism operates only through explicit physical forces without any biochemistry or internal state variables, our results present generic and far-reaching design principles, setting the stage for the next generation of synthetic nanomachines.
